verses.note: Most Christian interpreters from the early church on have also read Jesus' use of the verse of his return in glory (Matthew 24:30; Revelation 1:7). The two readings are often combined: the enthronement Daniel describes is made visible to the world when Christ comes.

Whatever event ‘comes’ names here (the resurrection, the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, or the final return), the verse ties the church's mission to Israel to the coming of the Son of Man and says the mission will not be finished first. It gives the persecuted a reason to keep moving rather than a date to calculate.

The harvest points to the end of the age, when the hidden growth of the kingdom will be gathered in. The time between sowing and harvest is not empty; the kingdom is growing, and the harvest will come at God's appointed moment.

Jesus speaks of his coming in the Father's glory with the angels as judge, and he makes the present stance of a person toward him decisive for that day. The verse holds together the lowly one who will be rejected and the coming one who will judge.
The cosmic signs prepare for the coming of the Son of Man in verse 26. Whether they describe the end of the world or the end of an age, they announce that God is acting decisively.

On the majority reading, the verse describes the visible, personal return of Christ in glory, the hope the Nicene Creed confesses when it says that Christ will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead.
The creeds confess that Christ will come again but set no date, following verse 32. The difficulty of verse 30 has pressed the church to read the chapter carefully rather than to speculate.
The return of Christ is certain in fact and uncertain in date. Every date-setter in the church's history has run against this verse.
The master will come, and his coming will be sudden. Readiness for Christ's return is expressed in wakefulness now.

The verse speaks of the Son of Man's coming in glory as the moment when present faithfulness or shame is answered. The return of Christ in Luke is not only a hope but a standard by which disciples measure what they will risk now.

The Son of Man acts as advocate or witness at the final judgment. What a person does with Jesus before others now has its counterpart when he comes in glory (9:26), the scene of Daniel 7:9-14, where the court sits before the Ancient of Days.

Waiting for the Lord's return is active: dressed for work, lamps trimmed, ears open for the knock. Luke's verb for waiting links the church's hope to Israel's faithful who waited for the consolation of Israel.

The returning master serves his servants. Luke's picture of the second coming is not only of judgment but of the Lord's astonishing humility, which he showed at the Last Supper (22:27) and will show at the banquet of his kingdom (22:30).

The Son of Man's coming is certain but its hour unknown. The early church took up this image of the thief in the night to describe the Lord's return (1 Thessalonians 5:2, 2 Peter 3:10, Revelation 3:3, 16:15), so the saying stands at the root of the New Testament's teaching on readiness.

The master's return brings reward as well as reckoning. The reward for faithful service is greater responsibility, as in the parable of the minas (19:17), which suggests that the age to come is a life of service, not idleness.

The delay of the Lord's coming is a test, and the servant fails it by assuming he has time. The New Testament answers the problem of delay the same way: the Lord is not slow, but patient, and his day will come unexpectedly (2 Peter 3:8-10).

The Son of Man's coming will be public and universal, not local or hidden. The verse is the basis for the church's confession that Christ will come again visibly, and it warns against any claim of a secret return.

The Son of Man's coming is called a revealing: he is not absent but hidden, and that day will unveil him. The verse gives the church its vocabulary for the second coming as apokalypsis, the unveiling of the one who already reigns.

The Son of Man's coming separates people who seemed to share the same situation. Readers who see a rapture here and readers who see the taken as swept away in judgment agree on the verse's point: readiness cannot be borrowed from the person next to you.

The parable is set within the expectation of the Son of Man's coming, and the vindication of God's people is tied to that day. Prayer is the posture of the church between the ascension and the return.

The nobleman goes, receives the kingdom, and comes back. Luke's readers knew the shape: Jesus goes to the Father, is exalted to the right hand of God (Acts 2:33-36), and will come again (Acts 1:11). The parable puts the whole time of the church inside the words ‘and then return’.

Faithfulness during the king's absence is what the returning king rewards, and the reward is a share in his rule. The New Testament elsewhere speaks of disciples reigning with Christ (Luke 22:29-30, 2 Timothy 2:12), and this parable pictures that reign as responsibility, not retirement.

Jesus classes announcements that ‘the time is near’ among the marks of deceivers. Christians confess that he will return, but this verse forbids following anyone who claims to know the time, a warning the church's long record of failed predictions has confirmed.

The signs precede the coming of the Son of Man and are described in the language of cosmic upheaval. Interpreters differ on how literally to take it: some expect physical signs in the heavens, others read the prophets' idiom for the fall of powers, as when Isaiah used it of Babylon. All agree that Luke presents the end as God's act that shakes the whole created order.

Luke's single cloud ties the coming of the Son of Man to the ascension, where a cloud took Jesus from sight and angels promised he would come in the same way (Acts 1:9-11). The church's creeds confess from texts like this that Christ will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead. Preterist interpreters, such as N. T. Wright, read the verse, with Daniel 7, chiefly as Jesus' vindication before God; most interpreters in the church's history have read it of his personal return.

For the disciples the return of Christ is not terror but release. The same events that make the world faint make them straighten up. Luke's word apolutrōsis, ‘redemption’, recalls those in the temple who waited for the redemption of Jerusalem (2:38), and Paul uses it for the redemption of the body still awaited (Romans 8:23).

Readers differ on verse 32. Preterist interpreters take ‘all things’ as the events up to AD 70; futurist interpreters take ‘this generation’ as the one that sees the final signs; mixed readings separate the signs and the city's fall from the coming itself. The chapter note sets out the views and their defenders. Verse 33 stands behind all of them: whatever the timing, the word is certain.

Most interpreters, among them D. A. Carson and Raymond Brown, hear in this verse Jesus' return at the end of the age, though the chapter also speaks of his coming in the resurrection (14:18-19) and through the Spirit (14:23). Dispensational writers such as John Walvoord (The Rapture Question, 1957) read it with 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17 as a promise that believers will be caught up to meet the Lord before a final tribulation; other Protestant, Catholic, and Orthodox readers take it of the one public return of Christ. All agree on what the verse itself stresses, that the end of the story is being with Jesus.

Jesus speaks of his coming as certain, ‘until I come’, while refusing to attach it to any person's lifespan or any date. The narrator's correction warns against building expectations about the time of the return on words that do not say what we wish.

The day of judgment is the day when Christ, who died and rose, acts as God's appointed judge. The one who will judge is the one the gospel offers as Savior, which is why Paul can call even the judgment ‘my gospel’.
The resurrection of believers takes place ‘at His coming’. Paul ties the general resurrection to Christ's return, not to each believer's death.

Christ's return brings both resurrection for the dead and transformation for the living, at the same instant. Paul's parallel description in 1 Thessalonians 4:15-17 adds that the living will not go before the dead.
Christ ‘will appear a second time’. His first coming dealt with sin; his second will bring salvation to completion for those who wait for him, so the church lives between the two appearances.
‘The coming one will come and will not delay.’ The return of Christ is presented as near and certain, the horizon that makes endurance reasonable.
